propositions.text: In the 1950s, BC government authorized Kenney Dam altering Nechako River flows used by CSTC First Nations without consultation.
propositions.quote: In the 1950s, the government of British Columbia authorized the building of the Kenney Dam in Northwest British Columbia for the production of hydro power for the smelting of aluminum. The dam and reservoir altered the water flows to the Nechako River, which the Carrier Sekani Tribal Council (“CSTC”) First Nations have since time immemorial used for fishing and sustenance. This was done without consulting with the CSTC First Nations.

propositions.text: Whether BC Utilities Commission must consider consultation with CSTC First Nations in approving power sale to BC Hydro.
propositions.quote: The question is whether the British Columbia Utilities Commission (the “Commission”) is required to consider the issue of consultation with the CSTC First Nations in determining whether the sale is in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states BC built Kenney Dam without consulting CSTC First Nations and asks if the Commission must consider consultation in power sale approval.

propositions.text: Haida Nation affirmed governments' duty to consult Aboriginal groups when decisions may adversely impact their lands and resources.
propositions.quote: In Haida Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2004 SCC 73, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 511, this Court affirmed that governments have a duty to consult with Aboriginal groups when making decisions which may adversely impact lands and resources to which Aboriginal peoples lay claim.

propositions.text: Consultation has become important in BC resource development due to land claims negotiations.
propositions.quote: In the intervening years, government-Aboriginal consultation has become an important part of the resource development process in British Columbia especially; much of the land and resources there are subject to land claims negotiations.

propositions.text: This case raises what triggers duty to consult and role of government tribunals in consultation and review.
propositions.quote: This case raises the issues of what triggers a duty to consult, and the place of government tribunals in consultation and the review of consultation.

propositions.text: I would allow the appeal but affirm BC Hydro's duty to consult CSTC First Nations on future developments affecting their claims.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal, while affirming the duty of BC Hydro to consult the CSTC First Nations on future developments that may adversely affect their claims and rights.

paragraphs.summary: The Court recalls Haida Nation's duty to consult, notes consultation's importance in BC, raises consultation issues, and would allow appeal affirming BC Hydro's duty.

propositions.text: In 1950s, Alcan dammed Nechako River for power for aluminum smelting, diverting water affecting CSTC fisheries.
propositions.quote: In the 1950s, Alcan (now Rio Tinto Alcan) dammed the Nechako River in northwestern British Columbia for the purposes of power development in connection with aluminum production. The project was one of huge magnitude. It diverted water from the Nechako River into the Nechako Reservoir, where a powerhouse was installed for the production of electricity. After passing through the turbines of the powerhouse, the water flowed to the Kemano River and on to the Pacific Ocean to the west. The dam affected the amount and timing of water flows into the Nechako River to the east, impacting fisheries on lands now claimed by the CSTC First Nations.

propositions.text: Alcan's water diversion was authorized by Final Water Licence No. 102324 granting permanent water use.
propositions.quote: Alcan effected these water diversions under Final Water Licence No. 102324 which gives Alcan use of the water on a permanent basis.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Alcan dammed Nechako River in 1950s affecting CSTC fisheries under a permanent water licence.

propositions.text: In 1987, Alcan, BC, and Canada agreed on water release to protect fish stocks; Canada involved due to federal fisheries jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Alcan, the Province of British Columbia, and Canada entered into a Settlement Agreement in 1987 on the release of waters in order to protect fish stocks. Canada was involved because fisheries, whether seacoast-based or inland, fall within federal jurisdiction under s. 91(12) of the Constitution Act, 1867 .

propositions.text: The 1987 agreement directs additional water flows in July and August to protect migrating salmon.
propositions.quote: The 1987 agreement directs the release of additional flows in July and August to protect migrating salmon.

propositions.text: A protocol between Haisla Nation and Alcan regulates water flows to protect eulachon spawning grounds.
propositions.quote: In addition, a protocol has been entered into between the Haisla Nation and Alcan which regulates water flows to protect eulachon spawning grounds.

paragraphs.summary: The Court describes the 1987 water release agreement involving Alcan, BC, Canada, and a protocol with Haisla Nation to protect fish.

propositions.text: Since 1961, Alcan sold excess power to BC Hydro; 2007 EPA commits supply until 2034 and creates Joint Operating Committee.
propositions.quote: Since 1961, however, Alcan has sold its excess power to BC Hydro, a Crown Corporation, for use in the local area and later for transmission to neighbouring communities. The Energy Purchase Agreement (“EPA”) entered into in 2007, which is the subject of this appeal is the latest in a series of power sales from Alcan to BC Hydro. It commits Alcan to supplying and BC Hydro to purchasing excess electricity from the Kemano site until 2034. The 2007 EPA establishes a Joint Operating Committee to advise the parties on the administration of the EPA and the operation of the reservoir.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Alcan has sold excess power to BC Hydro since 1961; 2007 EPA commits supply until 2034 with a Joint Operating Committee.

propositions.text: CSTC First Nations claim Nechako Valley as ancestral homeland and right to fish; were not consulted about 1950s dam.
propositions.quote: The CSTC First Nations claim the Nechako Valley as their ancestral homeland, and the right to fish in the Nechako River. As was the practice at the time, they were not consulted about the diversion of the river effected by the 1950s dam project.

propositions.text: CSTC argues 2007 EPA should be subject to consultation as a constitutional right under s. 35 of Constitution Act, 1982.
propositions.quote: They assert, however, that the 2007 EPA for the power generated by the project should be subject to consultation. This, they say, is their constitutional right under s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 , as defined in Haida Nation.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states CSTC claims ancestral rights and argues 2007 EPA requires consultation under s. 35 Constitution Act, 1982.

propositions.text: 2007 EPA was reviewed by Commission to determine if sale was in public interest under s. 71 Utilities Commission Act.
propositions.quote: The 2007 EPA was subject to review before the Commission. It was charged with determining whether the sale of electricity was in the public interest under s. 71 of the Utilities Commission Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 473.

propositions.text: Commission could declare contract unenforceable if not in public interest considering energy quantity, availability, price, and other relevant factors.
propositions.quote: The Commission had the power to declare a contract for the sale of electricity unenforceable if it found that it was not in the public interest having regard to the quantity of energy to be supplied, the availability of supplies, the price and availability of any other form of energy, the price of the energy supplied to a public utility company, and “any other factor that the commission considers relevant to the public interest”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court explains Commission's role to review 2007 EPA for public interest and power to reject contract if not in public interest.

propositions.text: Commission held procedural conferences to determine hearing scope and role of First Nations in proceedings.
propositions.quote: The Commission began its work by holding two procedural conferences to determine, among other things, the “scope” of its hearing.

propositions.text: CSTC was not party; Haisla Nation was and submitted Province and BC Hydro failed legal obligations but did not ask Commission to assess consultation adequacy.
propositions.quote: The CSTC was not party to the proceedings but the Haisla Nation was. The Haisla people submitted that the Province and BC Hydro “ha[d] failed to act on their legal obligation” to them, but refrained from asking the Commission “to assess the adequacy [of consultation] and accommodation afforded . . . on the 2007 EPA”

propositions.text: Commission's Scoping Order said insufficient consultation evidence is generally not determinative of matters before Commission.
propositions.quote: Generally, insufficient evidence of consultation, including with First Nations is not determinative of matters before the Commission.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission scoped hearing, CSTC not party, Haisla alleged legal failures but did not ask consultation assessment, and Commission found insufficient consultation evidence not determinative.

propositions.text: CSTC requested late intervener status on consultation issue due to potential negative impact on Aboriginal rights claims.
propositions.quote: On October 29, 2007, the CSTC requested late intervener status on the issue of consultation on the basis that the Commission’s decision might negatively impact Aboriginal rights and title which were the subject of its ongoing land claims.

propositions.text: At hearing opening, CSTC applied for reconsideration to include duty to consult, infringement, and environmental impact issues in hearing scope.
propositions.quote: At the opening of the oral hearing on November 19, 2007, the CSTC applied for reconsideration of the Scoping Order and, in written submissions of November 20, 2007, it asked the Commission to include in the hearing’s scope the issues of whether the duty to consult had been met, whether the proposed power sale under the 2007 EPA could constitute an infringement of Aboriginal rights and title in and of itself, and the related issue of the environmental impact of the 2007 EPA on the rights of the CSTC First Nations.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states CSTC sought late intervener status and applied for reconsideration to include consultation and infringement issues in hearing scope.

propositions.text: Commission used two-stage process for CSTC reconsideration: screening for evidentiary basis, then arguments on rescoping application.
propositions.quote: The Commission established a two-stage process to consider the CSTC’s application for reconsideration of the Scoping Order: an initial screening phase to determine whether there was a reasonable evidentiary basis for reconsideration, and a second phase to receive arguments on whether the rescoping application should be granted.

propositions.text: At first stage, CSTC filed evidence, called and cross-examined witnesses; proceedings confined to whether 2007 EPA would affect water flows or reservoir levels.
propositions.quote: At the first stage, the CSTC filed evidence, called witnesses and cross-examined the witnesses of BC Hydro and Alcan. The Commission confined the proceedings to the question of whether the 2007 EPA would adversely affect potential CSTC First Nations’ interests by causing changes in water flows into the Nechako River or changes in water levels of the Nechako Reservoir.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission used two-stage reconsideration process, with evidence and cross-examination confined to water flow impacts.

propositions.text: Commission found Alcan remains responsible for reservoir operation; 2007 EPA does not affect water levels or priority for water.
propositions.quote: It concluded that the “responsibility for operation of the Nechako Reservoir remains with Alcan under the 2007 EPA”, and that the EPA would not affect water levels in the Nechako River stating, “the 2007 EPA sets the priority of generation produced but does not set the priority for water”.

propositions.text: Alcan operates reservoir to optimize power generation regardless of 2007 EPA.
propositions.quote: With or without the 2007 EPA, “Alcan operates the Nechako Reservoir to optimize power generation”.

paragraphs.summary: The Court reports Commission found Alcan controls reservoir operation and 2007 EPA does not affect water levels or water priority.

propositions.text: Commission found fishery priority releases from reservoir are first to fish flows, second to power service under 1987 agreement.
propositions.quote: the priority of releases from the Nechako Reservoir [under the 1987 Settlement Agreement] is first to fish flows and second to power service

propositions.text: Timing changes in water releases for power generation under 2007 EPA have no impact on Nechako River releases relevant to CSTC.
propositions.quote: that change “will have no impact on the releases into the Nechako river system”.

propositions.text: Water releases for power flow into Kemano River west, not Nechako River east, so 2007 EPA does not affect CSTC concerns.
propositions.quote: This is because water releases for power generation flow not into the Nechako River system to the east, with which the CSTC First Nations are concerned, but into the Kemano River to the west.

propositions.text: 2007 EPA does not change control over water flows or reservoir management structure.
propositions.quote: Nor, the Commission found, would the 2007 EPA bring about a change in control over water flows and water levels, or alter the management structure of the reservoir.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission found 2007 EPA does not impact Nechako River fishery flows or control over water management relevant to CSTC.

propositions.text: Commission invited written submissions on whether not revising Scoping Order on consultation was jurisdictional error.
propositions.quote: The Commission then embarked on Phase II of the rescoping hearing and invited the parties to make written submissions on the reconsideration application — specifically, on whether it would be a jurisdictional error not to revise the Scoping Order to encompass consultation issues on these facts.

propositions.text: Parties made written submissions on the consultation rescoping application.
propositions.quote: The parties did so.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission invited and received written submissions on whether excluding consultation issues was jurisdictional error.

propositions.text: Commission dismissed CSTC reconsideration application, assuming historic infringement and consultation failure but requiring new adverse effect from 2007 EPA.
propositions.quote: For the purposes of the motion, the Commission assumed the historic infringement of Aboriginal rights, Aboriginal title, and a failure by the government to consult. Referring to Haida Nation, it concluded that “more than just an underlying infringement” was required. The CSTC had to demonstrate that the 2007 EPA would “adversely affect” the Aboriginal interests of its member First Nations.

propositions.text: Commission found section 71 review does not approve or change licenses; no new physical impacts means no jurisdictional error without consultation.
propositions.quote: Applying this test to its findings of fact, it stated that “a section 71 review does not approve, transfer or change control of licenses or authorization and therefore where there are no new physical impacts acceptance of a section 71 filing [without consultation] would not be a jurisdictional error”.

propositions.text: Commission concluded 2007 EPA would have no adverse effects on CSTC interests; duty to consult not triggered; no jurisdictional error in excluding consultation.
propositions.quote: The Commission therefore concluded that its decision on the 2007 EPA would have no adverse effects on the CSTC First Nations’ interests. The duty to consult was therefore not triggered, and no jurisdictional error was committed in failing to include consultation with the First Nations in the Scoping Order beyond the general consultation extended to all stakeholders.

paragraphs.summary: The Court reports Commission dismissed CSTC reconsideration, finding no new adverse effects or duty to consult, so no jurisdictional error.

propositions.text: Commission found 2007 EPA in public interest and evidence on consultation about historic infringement not helpful due to limited scope and no new impacts.
propositions.quote: The Commission went on to conclude that the 2007 EPA was in the public interest and should be accepted. It stated: In the circumstances of this review, evidence regarding consultation with respect to the historical, continuing infringement can reasonably be expected to be of no assistance for the same reasons there is no jurisdictional error, that is, the limited scope of the section 71 review, and there are no new physical impacts.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission found 2007 EPA in public interest and consultation evidence on historic infringement unhelpful due to limited review scope.

propositions.text: Commission viewed 2007 EPA as having no physical impact on Nechako River water levels or fishery management.
propositions.quote: In essence, the Commission took the view that the 2007 EPA would have no physical impact on the existing water levels in the Nechako River and hence it would not change the current management of its fishery.

propositions.text: Commission found decision would not transfer or change project licenses or operations, so no adverse impact on CSTC claims or rights.
propositions.quote: The Commission further found that its decision would not involve any transfer or change in the project’s licences or operations. Consequently, the Commission concluded that its decision would have no adverse impact on the pending claims or rights of the CSTC First Nations such that there was no need to rescope the hearing to permit further argument on the duty to consult.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Commission found no physical impact or license change from 2007 EPA, so no adverse impact or need to rescope for consultation.

propositions.text: CSTC appealed Commission's Reconsideration Decision and EPA approval to BC Court of Appeal.
propositions.quote: The CSTC appealed the Reconsideration Decision and the approval of the 2007 EPA to the British Columbia Court of Appeal.

propositions.text: BC Court of Appeal reversed Commission orders and remitted for evidence and argument on duty to consult and accommodation regarding 2007 EPA.
propositions.quote: The Court, per Donald J.A., reversed the Commission’s orders and remitted the case back to the Commission for “evidence and argument on whether a duty to consult and, if necessary, accommodate the [CSTC First Nations] exists and, if so, whether the duty has been met in respect of the filing of the 2007 EPA” (para. 69).

paragraphs.summary: The Court states CSTC appealed and BC Court of Appeal reversed Commission, remitting for consultation evidence and argument.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal found Commission had jurisdiction to consider consultation and constitutional issues.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal found that the Commission had jurisdiction to consider the issue of consultation. The Commission had the power to decide questions of law, and hence constitutional issues relating to the duty to consult.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Court of Appeal found Commission had jurisdiction to consider consultation and constitutional issues.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held Commission erred by prematurely rejecting reconsideration application without full hearing on consultation.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal went on to hold that the Commission acted prematurely by rejecting the application for reconsideration.

propositions.text: Commission erred by requiring CSTC to prove it would win consultation point before hearing it.
propositions.quote: The logic flaw was in predicting that consultation could have produced no useful outcome. Put another way, the Commission required a demonstration that the [CSTC] would win the point as a precondition for a hearing into the very same point.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal did not say Commission must find duty to consult, only that issue deserved full hearing.
propositions.quote: I do not say that the Commission would be bound to find a duty to consult here. The fault in the Commission’s decision is in not entertaining the issue of consultation within the scope of a full hearing when the circumstances demanded an inquiry.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Court of Appeal found Commission erred by prematurely rejecting consultation reconsideration without full hearing.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal held honour of Crown requires Commission to assess adequacy of consultation.
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal held that the honour of the Crown obliged the Commission to decide the consultation issue, and that “the tribunal with the power to approve the plan must accept the responsibility to assess the adequacy of consultation” (para. 53).

propositions.text: Court of Appeal did not consider whether 2007 EPA could adversely impact CSTC claims, nor criticize Commission's adverse impact finding.
propositions.quote: Unlike the Commission, the Court of Appeal did not consider whether the 2007 EPA was capable of having an adverse impact on a pending claim or right of the CSTC First Nations. The Court of Appeal did not criticize the Commission’s adverse impacts finding.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal took broader view than Commission on when duty to consult may arise, focusing on whether consultation could be useful.
propositions.quote: Rather, it appears to have concluded that despite these findings, the Commission was obliged to consider whether consultation could be “useful”. In finding that the Commission should have considered the consultation issue, the Court of Appeal appears to have taken a broader view than did the Commission as to when a duty to consult may arise.

paragraphs.summary: The Court states Court of Appeal held Commission must assess consultation adequacy, took broader view on duty to consult than Commission.

propositions.text: Court of Appeal suggested failure to consider consultation risks approving contract breaching Crown's constitutional duty
propositions.quote: The Court of Appeal suggested that a failure to consider consultation risked the approval of a contract in breach of the Crown’s constitutional duty.

propositions.text: Donald J.A. said breach allegation must be part of public interest inquiry
propositions.quote: Donald J.A. asked, “How can a contract formed by a Crown agent in breach of a constitutional duty be in the public interest? The existence of such a duty and the allegation of the breach must form part and parcel of the public interest inquiry” (para. 42).

paragraphs.summary: The Court of Appeal found failure to consider consultation risks approving a contract breaching Crown's duty; Donald J.A. said breach allegation must be part of public interest inquiry.

propositions.text: Alcan and BC Hydro argue Court of Appeal took too wide a view of Crown's duty to consult and tribunal's role
propositions.quote: They argue that the Court of Appeal took too wide a view of the Crown’s duty to consult and of the role of tribunals in deciding consultation issues.

propositions.text: Commission correctly concluded no duty to consider consultation issue for 2007 EPA
propositions.quote: Alcan and BC Hydro submit that the Commission correctly concluded that it had no duty to consider the consultation issue raised by the CSTC, since, however much participation was accorded, there was no possibility of finding a duty to consult with respect to the 2007 EPA.

paragraphs.summary: Alcan and BC Hydro argue Court of Appeal took too broad view of duty to consult and tribunal role; Commission correctly found no duty to consider consultation for 2007 EPA.

propositions.text: CSTC argues Court of Appeal correctly held Commission erred in refusing to rescope proceeding to allow consultation submissions
propositions.quote: The CSTC argues that the Court of Appeal correctly held that the Commission erred in refusing to rescope its proceeding to allow submissions on the consultation issue.

propositions.text: CSTC does not pursue earlier procedural arguments in this Court
propositions.quote: It does not pursue earlier procedural arguments in this Court.

paragraphs.summary: CSTC argues Court of Appeal rightly held Commission erred by refusing to rescope proceeding for consultation submissions; does not pursue earlier procedural arguments.

propositions.text: 2007 EPA reviewed under s. 71 Utilities Commission Act for public interest based on specified factors
propositions.quote: The 2007 EPA was subject to review before the Commission under the authority of s. 71 of the Utilities Commission Act to determine whether it was in the public interest.

propositions.text: Prior to May 2008, public interest factors included energy quantity, availability, price, and other relevant factors
propositions.quote: Prior to May 2008, this determination was to be based on the quantity of energy to be supplied; the availability of supplies; the price and availability of any other form of energy; the price of the energy supplied to a public utility company; and “any other factor that the commission considers relevant to the public interest”: Utilities Commission Act, s. 71(2)(a) to (e).

propositions.text: Effective May 2008, considerations expanded to include government energy objectives and long-term resource plans
propositions.quote: Effective May 2008, these considerations were expanded to include “the government’s energy objectives” and its long-term resource plans: s. 71(2.1)(a) and (b).

propositions.text: Public interest clause narrowed to interests of potential BC public utility customers
propositions.quote: The public interest clause, however, was narrowed to considerations of the interests of potential British Columbia public utility customers: s. 71(2.1)(d).

paragraphs.summary: The 2007 EPA was reviewed under s. 71 Utilities Commission Act for public interest, with factors expanded in May 2008 to include government energy objectives and narrowed to BC public utility customers' interests.

propositions.text: Commission may approve contract if in public interest under s. 71(2.4) Utilities Commission Act
propositions.quote: Based on the above considerations, the Commission may issue an order approving the proposed contract under s. 71(2.4) of the Utilities Commission Act if it is found to be in the public interest.

propositions.text: If not in public interest, Commission can declare contract unenforceable or make other orders
propositions.quote: If it is not found to be in the public interest, the Commission can issue an order declaring the contract unenforceable, either wholly or in part, or “make any other order it considers advisable in the circumstances”: s. 71(2) and (3).

paragraphs.summary: Commission may approve contract if in public interest; if not, can declare contract unenforceable or make other orders under Utilities Commission Act.

propositions.text: Section 79 Utilities Commission Act makes Commission's fact findings binding and conclusive
propositions.quote: Section 79 of the Utilities Commission Act states that all findings of fact made by the Commission within its jurisdiction are “binding and conclusive”.

propositions.text: Section 105 grants Commission exclusive jurisdiction in matters conferred by any Act
propositions.quote: This is supplemented by s. 105 which grants the Commission “exclusive jurisdiction in all cases and for all matters in which jurisdiction is conferred on it by this or any other Act”.

propositions.text: Appeal lies from Commission decision or order to Court of Appeal with leave under s. 101(1)
propositions.quote: An appeal, however, lies from a decision or order of the Commission to the Court of Appeal with leave: s. 101(1).

paragraphs.summary: Section 79 makes Commission's fact findings binding; s. 105 grants exclusive jurisdiction; appeal lies to Court of Appeal with leave.

propositions.text: Sections 79 and 105 constitute a privative clause under British Columbia Administrative Tribunals Act
propositions.quote: Together, ss. 79 and 105 of the Utilities Commission Act constitute a “privative clause” as defined in s. 1 of the British Columbia Administrative Tribunals Act, S.B.C. 2004, c. 45.

propositions.text: Privative clause attracts patently unreasonable standard of judicial review for tribunal's findings within exclusive jurisdiction
propositions.quote: Under s. 58 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, this privative clause attracts a “patently unreasonable” standard of judicial review to “a finding of fact or law or an exercise of discretion by the tribunal in respect of a matter over which it has exclusive jurisdiction under a privative clause”; a standard of correctness is to be applied in the review of “all [other] matters”.

paragraphs.summary: Sections 79 and 105 form a privative clause attracting patently unreasonable review for tribunal's exclusive jurisdiction findings; correctness standard applies otherwise.

propositions.text: Section 44(1) Administrative Tribunals Act states tribunal lacks jurisdiction over constitutional questions
propositions.quote: Section 44(1) of the Administrative Tribunals Act states that “[t]he tribunal does not have jurisdiction over constitutional questions”.

propositions.text: Section 44(1) applies to Commission by virtue of s. 2(4) Utilities Commission Act
propositions.quote: which applies to the Commission by virtue of s. 2(4) of the Utilities Commission Act.

propositions.text: Constitutional question defined by s. 1 Administrative Tribunals Act via s. 8 Constitutional Question Act
propositions.quote: A “constitutional question” is defined in s. 1 of the Administrative Tribunals Act by s. 8 of the Constitutional Question Act, R.S.B.C. 1996, c. 68.

propositions.text: Section 8(2) Constitutional Question Act requires notice to Attorneys General before holding law invalid or granting constitutional remedy
propositions.quote: Section 8(2) says: 8. . . . (2) If in a cause, matter or other proceeding (a) the constitutional validity or constitutional applicability of any law is challenged, or (b) an application is made for a constitutional remedy, the law must not be held to be invalid or inapplicable and the remedy must not be granted until after notice of the challenge or application has been served on the Attorney General of Canada and the Attorney General of British Columbia in accordance with this section.

propositions.text: Constitutional remedy defined as remedy under s. 24(1) Charter excluding exclusion of evidence or consequential remedies
propositions.quote: A “constitutional remedy” is defined as “a remedy under section 24(1) of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms other than a remedy consisting of the exclusion of evidence or consequential on such exclusion”: Constitutional Question Act, s. 8(1).

paragraphs.summary: Section 44(1) Administrative Tribunals Act denies tribunal jurisdiction over constitutional questions; notice required before invalidating law or granting constitutional remedy.

propositions.text: Section 35 Constitution Act, 1982 recognizes and affirms existing aboriginal and treaty rights
propositions.quote: Section 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 reads: 35. (1) The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.

propositions.text: Section 35 defines aboriginal peoples to include Indian, Inuit and Métis peoples
propositions.quote: (2) In this Act, “aboriginal peoples of Canada” includes the Indian, Inuit and Métis peoples of Canada.

propositions.text: Section 35 clarifies treaty rights include land claims agreements rights
propositions.quote: (3) For greater certainty, in subsection (1) “treaty rights” includes rights that now exist by way of land claims agreements or may be so acquired.

propositions.text: Section 35 guarantees aboriginal and treaty rights equally to male and female persons
propositions.quote: (4) Notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, the aboriginal and treaty rights referred to in subsection (1) are guaranteed equally to male and female persons.

paragraphs.summary: Section 35 Constitution Act, 1982 recognizes and affirms aboriginal and treaty rights, defines aboriginal peoples, includes land claims, and guarantees rights equally by gender.

propositions.text: Main issues: Commission's jurisdiction to consider consultation and refusal to rescope inquiry
propositions.quote: The main issues that must be resolved are: (1) whether the Commission had jurisdiction to consider consultation; and (2) if so, whether the Commission’s refusal to rescope the inquiry to consider consultation should be set aside.

propositions.text: To resolve issues, necessary to consider when duty to consult arises and tribunals' role
propositions.quote: In order to resolve these issues, it is necessary to consider when a duty to consult arises and the role of tribunals in relation to the duty to consult.

propositions.text: Reasons will consider five topics including duty to consult, tribunals' role, Commission's jurisdiction, reconsideration decision, and public interest conclusion
propositions.quote: These reasons will therefore consider: 1. When a duty to consult arises; 2. The role of tribunals in consultation; 3. The Commission’s jurisdiction to consider consultation; 4. The Commission’s Reconsideration Decision; 5. The Commission’s conclusion that approval of the 2007 EPA was in the public interest.

paragraphs.summary: Main issues are Commission's jurisdiction to consider consultation and refusal to rescope inquiry; reasons will consider duty to consult, tribunals' role, and Commission's decisions.

propositions.text: Duty to consult arises when Crown knows of potential Aboriginal right and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it
propositions.quote: The Court in Haida Nation answered this question as follows: the duty to consult arises “when the Crown has knowledge, real or constructive, of the potential existence of the Aboriginal right or title and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it” (para. 35).

propositions.text: Test broken into three elements: Crown's knowledge, contemplated conduct, potential adverse effect
propositions.quote: This test can be broken down into three elements: (1) the Crown’s knowledge, actual or constructive, of a potential Aboriginal claim or right; (2) contemplated Crown conduct; and (3) the potential that the contemplated conduct may adversely affect an Aboriginal claim or right.

propositions.text: Will discuss each element in greater detail and general comments on duty's source and nature
propositions.quote: I will discuss each of these elements in greater detail. First, some general comments on the source and nature of the duty to consult are in order.

paragraphs.summary: Haida Nation holds duty to consult arises when Crown knows of potential Aboriginal right and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it; test has three elements.

propositions.text: Duty to consult grounded in honour of the Crown and obligation to settle Aboriginal claims
propositions.quote: The duty to consult is grounded in the honour of the Crown. It is a corollary of the Crown’s obligation to achieve the just settlement of Aboriginal claims through the treaty process.

propositions.text: While treaty claims ongoing, duty to consult and accommodate Aboriginal interests in spirit of reconciliation
propositions.quote: While the treaty claims process is ongoing, there is an implied duty to consult with the Aboriginal claimants on matters that may adversely affect their treaty and Aboriginal rights, and to accommodate those interests in the spirit of reconciliation: Haida Nation, at para. 20.

propositions.text: Haida Nation states Aboriginal peoples were here before Europeans, some reconciled claims by treaty, others not
propositions.quote: As stated in Haida Nation, at para. 25: Put simply, Canada’s Aboriginal peoples were here when Europeans came, and were never conquered. Many bands reconciled their claims with the sovereignty of the Crown through negotiated treaties. Others, notably in British Columbia, have yet to do so.

propositions.text: Potential rights protected by s. 35 Constitution Act, 1982; honour of Crown requires rights be determined, recognized, respected
propositions.quote: The potential rights embedded in these claims are protected by s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 . The honour of the Crown requires that these rights be determined, recognized and respected.

propositions.text: Honour of Crown requires honourable participation in negotiation and consultation with accommodation
propositions.quote: This, in turn, requires the Crown, acting honourably, to participate in processes of negotiation. While this process continues, the honour of the Crown may require it to consult and, where indicated, accommodate Aboriginal interests.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult is grounded in honour of Crown and obligation to settle Aboriginal claims; Haida Nation requires consultation and accommodation during ongoing treaty claims.

propositions.text: Duty to consult protects Aboriginal interests during ongoing claims to avoid costly litigation and injunctions
propositions.quote: The duty to consult described in Haida Nation derives from the need to protect Aboriginal interests while land and resource claims are ongoing or when the proposed action may impinge on an Aboriginal right.

propositions.text: Without duty, Aboriginal groups must seek injunctions which are time-consuming, expensive, and often ineffective
propositions.quote: Absent this duty, Aboriginal groups seeking to protect their interests pending a final settlement would need to commence litigation and seek interlocutory injunctions to halt the threatening activity. These remedies have proven time-consuming, expensive, and are often ineffective.

propositions.text: Many Aboriginal groups have limited success obtaining injunctions to halt development affecting rights
propositions.quote: Moreover, with a few exceptions, many Aboriginal groups have limited success in obtaining injunctions to halt development or activities on the land in order to protect contested Aboriginal or treaty rights.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult protects Aboriginal interests during ongoing claims to avoid costly, often ineffective litigation and injunctions.

propositions.text: Duty to consult has legal and constitutional character grounded in honour of Crown
propositions.quote: Grounded in the honour of the Crown, the duty has both a legal and a constitutional character: R. v. Kapp, 2008 SCC 41, [2008] 2 S.C.R. 483, at para. 6.

propositions.text: Duty seeks to protect Aboriginal rights and further reconciliation goals between Aboriginal peoples and Crown
propositions.quote: The duty seeks to provide protection to Aboriginal and treaty rights while furthering the goals of reconciliation between Aboriginal peoples and the Crown.

propositions.text: Duty recognizes need for cooperation rather than litigation between Aboriginal peoples and Crown
propositions.quote: Rather than pitting Aboriginal peoples against the Crown in the litigation process, the duty recognizes that both must work together to reconcile their interests.

propositions.text: Duty accommodates reality that Aboriginal peoples often involved in resource exploitation; injunctions may serve no one's interest
propositions.quote: It also accommodates the reality that often Aboriginal peoples are involved in exploiting the resource. Shutting down development by court injunction may serve the interest of no one.

propositions.text: Honour of Crown best reflected by consultation with view to reconciliation
propositions.quote: The honour of the Crown is therefore best reflected by a requirement for consultation with a view to reconciliation.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult has legal and constitutional basis, aims to protect rights and promote reconciliation, requiring cooperation and consultation rather than litigation.

propositions.text: Haida Nation requires Crown to consider contested or established Aboriginal rights before decisions affecting them
propositions.quote: Haida Nation sets the framework for dialogue prior to the final resolution of claims by requiring the Crown to take contested or established Aboriginal rights into account before making a decision that may have an adverse impact on them: J. Woodward, Native Law, vol. 1 (loose-leaf), at p. 5-35.

propositions.text: Duty is prospective, focusing on rights yet to be proven
propositions.quote: The duty is prospective, fastening on rights yet to be proven.

paragraphs.summary: Haida Nation requires Crown to consider Aboriginal rights before decisions affecting them; duty is prospective, focusing on unproven rights.

propositions.text: Nature of duty varies with strength of claim and seriousness of impact
propositions.quote: The nature of the duty varies with the situation. The richness of the required consultation increases with the strength of the prima facie Aboriginal claim and the seriousness of the impact on the underlying Aboriginal or treaty right: Haida Nation, at paras. 43‑45, and Taku River Tlingit First Nation v. British Columbia (Project Assessment Director), 2004 SCC 74, [2004] 3 S.C.R. 550, at para. 32.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult varies with strength of claim and seriousness of impact on Aboriginal or treaty right.

propositions.text: Remedies for breach of duty vary from injunctions to damages to orders to consult before proceeding
propositions.quote: The remedy for a breach of the duty to consult also varies with the situation. The Crown’s failure to consult can lead to a number of remedies ranging from injunctive relief against the threatening activity altogether, to damages, to an order to carry out the consultation prior to proceeding further with the proposed government conduct: Haida Nation, at paras. 13‑14.

paragraphs.summary: Remedies for breach of duty to consult vary from injunctions to damages to orders to consult before proceeding.

propositions.text: Duty to consult embodies a generative constitutional order serving a dynamic function under s. 35
propositions.quote: The duty to consult embodies what Brian Slattery has described as a “generative” constitutional order which sees “section 35 as serving a dynamic and not simply static function” (“Aboriginal Rights and the Honour of the Crown” (2005), 29 S.C.L.R. (2d) 433, at p. 440).

propositions.text: Haida Nation describes duty as part of ongoing reconciliation process beyond formal claims resolution
propositions.quote: This dynamicism was articulated in Haida Nation as follows, at para. 32: . . . the duty to consult and accommodate is part of a process of fair dealing and reconciliation that begins with the assertion of sovereignty and continues beyond formal claims resolution.

propositions.text: Consultation concerned with ongoing relationships and promotes ongoing negotiations
propositions.quote: As the post‑Haida Nation case law confirms, consultation is “[c]oncerned with an ethic of ongoing relationships” and seeks to further an ongoing process of reconciliation by articulating a preference for remedies “that promote ongoing negotiations”: D. G. Newman, The Duty to Consult: New Relationships with Aboriginal Peoples (2009), at p. 21.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult is a dynamic constitutional process promoting ongoing reconciliation and negotiations beyond formal claims resolution.

propositions.text: Now turning to three elements that give rise to duty to consult, starting with Crown's knowledge of potential claim or right
propositions.quote: Against this background, I now turn to the three elements that give rise to a duty to consult. (1) Knowledge by the Crown of a Potential Claim or Right

paragraphs.summary: Court will now analyze three elements giving rise to duty to consult, starting with Crown's knowledge of potential claim or right.

propositions.text: Duty to consult triggered by Crown's real or constructive knowledge of claim to resource or land
propositions.quote: To trigger the duty to consult, the Crown must have real or constructive knowledge of a claim to the resource or land to which it attaches: Haida Nation, at para. 35.

propositions.text: Actual knowledge arises when claim filed in court, advanced in negotiations, or treaty right may be impacted
propositions.quote: Actual knowledge arises when a claim has been filed in court or advanced in the context of negotiations, or when a treaty right may be impacted: Mikisew Cree First Nation v. Canada (Minister of Canadian Heritage), 2005 SCC 69, [2005] 3 S.C.R. 388, para. 34.

propositions.text: Constructive knowledge arises when lands known or reasonably suspected to be traditionally occupied or impact anticipated
propositions.quote: Constructive knowledge arises when lands are known or reasonably suspected to have been traditionally occupied by an Aboriginal community or an impact on rights may reasonably be anticipated.

propositions.text: Existence of potential claim essential but proof of success not required; credible claim suffices
propositions.quote: While the existence of a potential claim is essential, proof that the claim will succeed is not. What is required is a credible claim.

propositions.text: Tenuous claims may attract mere duty of notice; stronger claims attract more stringent duties
propositions.quote: Tenuous claims, for which a strong prima facie case is absent, may attract a mere duty of notice.

propositions.text: Knowledge of credible but unproven claim suffices to trigger duty to consult and accommodate
propositions.quote: As stated in Haida Nation, at para. 37: Knowledge of a credible but unproven claim suffices to trigger a duty to consult and accommodate.

paragraphs.summary: Duty to consult triggered by Crown's real or constructive knowledge of credible but unproven Aboriginal claim; stronger claims require more consultation.

propositions.text: The claim or right must actually exist and be affected by proposed government action to trigger consultation duty.
propositions.quote: The claim or right must be one which actually exists and stands to be affected by the proposed government action.

propositions.text: Consultation protects unproven or established rights from irreversible harm during settlement negotiations.
propositions.quote: This flows from the fact that the purpose of consultation is to protect unproven or established rights from irreversible harm as the settlement negotiations proceed: Newman, at p. 30, citing Haida Nation, at paras. 27 and 33.

paragraphs.summary: The court states consultation protects existing or potential rights from irreversible harm during settlement negotiations, requiring the claim to actually exist and be affected.

propositions.text: A duty to consult arises only if Crown conduct or decision engages a potential Aboriginal right and may adversely impact it.
propositions.quote: Second, for a duty to consult to arise, there must be Crown conduct or a Crown decision that engages a potential Aboriginal right. What is required is conduct that may adversely impact on the claim or right in question.

paragraphs.summary: The court states a duty to consult arises only if Crown conduct or decision may adversely impact a potential Aboriginal right.

propositions.text: Government action engaging duty to consult is not limited to statutory powers but includes broader conduct.
propositions.quote: It has been held that such action is not confined to government exercise of statutory powers: Huu-Ay-Aht First Nation v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2005 BCSC 697, [2005] 3 C.N.L.R. 74, at paras. 94 and 104; Wii’litswx v. British Columbia (Minister of Forests), 2008 BCSC 1139, [2008] 4 C.N.L.R. 315, at paras. 11-15.

propositions.text: A generous, purposive approach applies to the duty to consult.
propositions.quote: This accords with the generous, purposive approach that must be brought to the duty to consult.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains government action triggering duty to consult is not limited to statutory powers and requires a generous, purposive approach.

propositions.text: Government action includes strategic, higher-level decisions with potential impact on Aboriginal claims and rights.
propositions.quote: Further, government action is not confined to decisions or conduct which have an immediate impact on lands and resources. A potential for adverse impact suffices. Thus, the duty to consult extends to “strategic, higher level decisions” that may have an impact on Aboriginal claims and rights (Woodward, at p. 5-41 (emphasis omitted)).

propositions.text: Examples of government action triggering duty to consult include transfer of tree licences, forest management plans, pipeline review processes, and electricity transmission inquiries.
propositions.quote: Examples include the transfer of tree licences which would have permitted the cutting of old-growth forest (Haida Nation); the approval of a multi-year forest management plan for a large geographic area (Klahoose First Nation v. Sunshine Coast Forest District (District Manager), 2008 BCSC 1642, [2009] 1 C.N.L.R. 110); the establishment of a review process for a major gas pipeline (Dene Tha’ First Nation v. Canada (Minister of Environment), 2006 FC 1354, [2007] 1 C.N.L.R. 1, aff’d 2008 FCA 20, 35 C.E.L.R. (3d) 1); and the conduct of a comprehensive inquiry to determine a province’s infrastructure and capacity needs for electricity transmission (An Inquiry into British Columbia’s Electricity Transmission Infrastructure & Capacity Needs for the Next 30 Years, Re, 2009 CarswellBC 3637 (B.C.U.C.)).

propositions.text: Whether government conduct includes legislative action is left for future consideration.
propositions.quote: We leave for another day the question of whether government conduct includes legislative action: see R. v. Lefthand, 2007 ABCA 206, 77 Alta. L.R. (4th) 203, at paras. 37-40.

paragraphs.summary: The court states government action includes strategic decisions potentially impacting Aboriginal rights, gives examples, and defers on legislative action question.

propositions.text: A duty to consult requires a causal link between Crown conduct and potential adverse impact on Aboriginal claims or rights.
propositions.quote: The claimant must show a causal relationship between the proposed government conduct or decision and a potential for adverse impacts on pending Aboriginal claims or rights.

propositions.text: Past wrongs or previous breaches of duty to consult do not suffice to trigger duty to consult.
propositions.quote: Past wrongs, including previous breaches of the duty to consult, do not suffice.

paragraphs.summary: The court states duty to consult requires causal link between Crown conduct and potential adverse impact; past breaches alone do not suffice.

propositions.text: A generous, purposive approach applies to assessing adverse impact for duty to consult.
propositions.quote: Again, a generous, purposive approach to this element is in order, given that the doctrine’s purpose, as stated by Newman, is “to recognize that actions affecting unproven Aboriginal title or rights or treaty rights can have irreversible effects that are not in keeping with the honour of the Crown” (p. 30, citing Haida Nation, at paras. 27 and 33).

propositions.text: Mere speculative impacts do not suffice; there must be an appreciable adverse effect on the ability to exercise the Aboriginal right.
propositions.quote: Mere speculative impacts, however, will not suffice. As stated in R. v. Douglas, 2007 BCCA 265, 278 D.L.R. (4th) 653, at para. 44, there must an “appreciable adverse effect on the First Nations’ ability to exercise their aboriginal right”.

propositions.text: Adverse effect must be on future exercise of the right itself, not on negotiating position.
propositions.quote: The adverse effect must be on the future exercise of the right itself; an adverse effect on a First Nation’s future negotiating position does not suffice.

paragraphs.summary: The court states duty to consult requires appreciable adverse effect on future exercise of Aboriginal right, not speculative impacts or negotiating position.

propositions.text: Adverse impacts include any effect prejudicing pending Aboriginal claims or rights, including structural resource management changes.
propositions.quote: Adverse impacts extend to any effect that may prejudice a pending Aboriginal claim or right. Often the adverse effects are physical in nature. However, as discussed in connection with what constitutes Crown conduct, high-level management decisions or structural changes to the resource’s management may also adversely affect Aboriginal claims or rights even if these decisions have no “immediate impact on lands and resources”: Woodward, at p. 5-41.

propositions.text: Structural changes may set stage for further decisions adversely impacting land and resources.
propositions.quote: This is because such structural changes to the resources management may set the stage for further decisions that will have a direct adverse impact on land and resources.

propositions.text: Transfer of resource power from Crown to private party may diminish Aboriginal constitutional rights to have interests considered.
propositions.quote: For example, a contract that transfers power over a resource from the Crown to a private party may remove or reduce the Crown’s power to ensure that the resource is developed in a way that respects Aboriginal interests in accordance with the honour of the Crown. The Aboriginal people would thus effectively lose or find diminished their constitutional right to have their interests considered in development decisions.

propositions.text: Such adverse impact is recognized in Haida Nation at paras. 72-73.
propositions.quote: This is an adverse impact: see Haida Nation, at paras. 72-73.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains adverse impacts include structural resource management changes that may prejudice Aboriginal claims, including transfer of power reducing Crown's duty.

propositions.text: Continuing breaches are not adverse impacts for triggering duty to consult; duty aims to prevent damage during negotiations.
propositions.quote: An underlying or continuing breach, while remediable in other ways, is not an adverse impact for the purposes of determining whether a particular government decision gives rise to a duty to consult. The duty to consult is designed to prevent damage to Aboriginal claims and rights while claim negotiations are underway: Haida Nation, at para. 33.

propositions.text: Duty arises when Crown knows of potential or actual Aboriginal right and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it.
propositions.quote: The duty arises when the Crown has knowledge, real or constructive, of the potential or actual existence of the Aboriginal right or title “and contemplates conduct that might adversely affect it”: Haida Nation, at para. 35 (emphasis added).

propositions.text: Mikisew Cree confirms this test in treaty rights context.
propositions.quote: This test was confirmed by the Court in Mikisew Cree in the context of treaty rights, at paras. 33-34.

paragraphs.summary: The court states continuing breaches do not trigger duty to consult; duty arises when Crown contemplates conduct potentially adversely affecting Aboriginal rights.

propositions.text: Duty to consult triggers only if current government decision may cause novel adverse impact on present claim or right.
propositions.quote: Prior and continuing breaches, including prior failures to consult, will only trigger a duty to consult if the present decision has the potential of causing a novel adverse impact on a present claim or existing right.

propositions.text: Remedies exist for past breaches, including damages; fresh duty requires jeopardy to current claims and rights.
propositions.quote: As noted in Haida Nation, a breach of the duty to consult may be remedied in various ways, including the awarding of damages. To trigger a fresh duty of consultation — the matter which is here at issue — a contemplated Crown action must put current claims and rights in jeopardy.

paragraphs.summary: The court states fresh duty to consult arises only if current decision risks novel adverse impact; past breaches have other remedies.

propositions.text: Adverse effect does not include impacts on negotiating position of Aboriginal group.
propositions.quote: Nor does the definition of what constitutes an adverse effect extend to adverse impacts on the negotiating position of an Aboriginal group.

propositions.text: Duty to consult aims to protect Aboriginal rights and future resource use, not to give negotiation advantage.
propositions.quote: cut off from its roots in the need to preserve Aboriginal interests, its purpose would be reduced to giving one side in the negotiation process an advantage over the other.

propositions.text: Duty to consult may incidentally delay development but serves constitutional duties to First Nations.
propositions.quote: The duty to consult, grounded in the need to protect Aboriginal rights and to preserve the future use of the resources claimed by Aboriginal peoples while balancing countervailing Crown interests, no doubt may have the ulterior effect of delaying ongoing development.

paragraphs.summary: The court states adverse effect excludes impacts on negotiating position; duty to consult protects Aboriginal rights, not negotiation advantage.

propositions.text: Duty to consult arises when Crown knows of potential claims, proposes conduct, and conduct may adversely impact claims.
propositions.quote: As we have seen, the duty to consult arises when: (1) the Crown has knowledge, actual or constructive, of potential aboriginal claims or rights; (2) the Crown proposes conduct or a decision; and (3) that conduct or decision may have an adverse impact on the Aboriginal claims or rights.

propositions.text: A causal connection between proposed conduct and potential adverse impact is required.
propositions.quote: This requires demonstration of a causal connection between the proposed Crown conduct and a potential adverse impact on an Aboriginal claim or right.

paragraphs.summary: The court summarizes duty to consult elements: Crown knowledge, proposed conduct, and potential adverse impact with causal connection.

propositions.text: Duty to consult arises if any Crown action relates to a project impacting Aboriginal rights, even if current action has no impact.
propositions.quote: It argues that even if the 2007 EPA will have no impact on the Nechako River water levels, the Nechako fisheries or the management of the contested resource, the duty to consult may be triggered because the 2007 EPA is part of a larger hydro-electric project which continues to impact its rights.

propositions.text: Any current government action, however limited, triggers duty to consult on entire resource project.
propositions.quote: The current government action or decision, however inconsequential, becomes the hook that secures and reels in the constitutional duty to consult on the entire resource.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues any Crown action related to a project impacting rights triggers duty to consult on entire project, even if current action has no impact.

propositions.text: Court rejects broad view that duty to consult extends to entire project from any related Crown action.
propositions.quote: I cannot accept this view of the duty to consult.

propositions.text: Haida Nation confines duty to consult to adverse impacts from specific Crown proposal, not entire project.
propositions.quote: Haida Nation negates such a broad approach. It grounded the duty to consult in the need to preserve Aboriginal rights and claims pending resolution. It confines the duty to consult to adverse impacts flowing from the specific Crown proposal at issue — not to larger adverse impacts of the project of which it is a part.

propositions.text: Consultation subject is impact on claimed rights of current decision under consideration.
propositions.quote: The subject of the consultation is the impact on the claimed rights of the current decision under consideration.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects respondent's broad duty to consult view, holding duty is confined to adverse impacts from specific Crown proposal.

propositions.text: Respondent argues failure to consult on initial project requires consultation on entire resource and management.
propositions.quote: The argument for a broader duty to consult invokes the logic of the fruit of the poisoned tree — an evidentiary doctrine that holds that past wrongs preclude the Crown from subsequently benefiting from them. Thus, it is suggested that the failure to consult with the CSTC First Nations on the initial dam and water diversion project prevents any further development of that resource without consulting on the entirety of the resource and its management.

propositions.text: Court rejects this argument, stating failure to consult gives rise to remedies but consultation order requires potential adverse impact from proposed conduct.
propositions.quote: Yet, as Haida Nation pointed out, the failure to consult gives rise to a variety of remedies, including damages. An order compelling consultation is only appropriate where the proposed Crown conduct, immediate or prospective, may adversely impact on established or claimed rights. Absent this, other remedies may be more appropriate.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues failure to consult on initial project requires consultation on entire resource; court rejects, requiring potential adverse impact from proposed conduct.

propositions.text: Tribunal's duty to consider consultation depends on its legislative mandate.
propositions.quote: The duty on a tribunal to consider consultation and the scope of that inquiry depends on the mandate conferred by the legislation that creates the tribunal.

propositions.text: Tribunals have only powers conferred by their constituent legislation: R. v. Conway.
propositions.quote: Tribunals are confined to the powers conferred on them by their constituent legislation: R. v. Conway, 2010 SCC 22, [2010] 1 S.C.R. 765.

propositions.text: Role of tribunals in consultation depends on duties and powers legislature confers.
propositions.quote: It follows that the role of particular tribunals in relation to consultation depends on the duties and powers the legislature has conferred on it.

paragraphs.summary: The court states tribunal's duty to consider consultation depends on legislative mandate and powers conferred by statute.

propositions.text: Legislature may delegate Crown's duty to consult to a tribunal.
propositions.quote: The legislature may choose to delegate to a tribunal the Crown’s duty to consult.

propositions.text: Governments may set regulatory schemes addressing procedural consultation requirements at different decision stages: Haida Nation.
propositions.quote: As noted in Haida Nation, it is open to governments to set up regulatory schemes to address the procedural requirements of consultation at different stages of the decision‑making process with respect to a resource.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislature may delegate Crown's duty to consult to tribunals and governments may regulate consultation procedures.

propositions.text: Legislature may limit tribunal's role to reviewing adequacy of consultation as condition of decision-making.
propositions.quote: Alternatively, the legislature may choose to confine a tribunal’s power to determinations of whether adequate consultation has taken place, as a condition of its statutory decision-making process.

propositions.text: In such case, tribunal reviews Crown's discharge of duty but does not engage in consultation itself.
propositions.quote: In this case, the tribunal is not itself engaged in the consultation. Rather, it is reviewing whether the Crown has discharged its duty to consult with a given First Nation about potential adverse impacts on their Aboriginal interest relevant to the decision at hand.

paragraphs.summary: The court states legislature may confine tribunal to reviewing adequacy of consultation, not engaging in consultation itself.

propositions.text: Tribunals may have no duty, duty to consult, or duty to consider consultation depending on legislative conferral.
propositions.quote: Tribunals considering resource issues touching on Aboriginal interests may have neither of these duties, one of these duties, or both depending on what responsibilities the legislature has conferred on them.

propositions.text: Tribunal's powers and remedial powers are relevant to determining consultation duties and jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Both the powers of the tribunal to consider questions of law and the remedial powers granted it by the legislature are relevant considerations in determining the contours of that tribunal’s jurisdiction: Conway.

propositions.text: These considerations determine whether tribunal has duty to consult, consider consultation, or no duty.
propositions.quote: As such, they are also relevant to determining whether a particular tribunal has a duty to consult, a duty to consider consultation, or no duty at all.

paragraphs.summary: The court states tribunal's consultation duties depend on legislative powers and remedial authority conferred.

propositions.text: Argument that every tribunal with jurisdiction over legal questions has constitutional duty to consider and fulfill consultation.
propositions.quote: In particular, it is suggested that every tribunal with jurisdiction to consider questions of law has a constitutional duty to consider whether adequate consultation has taken place and, if not, to itself fulfill the requirement regardless of whether its constituent statute so provides.

propositions.text: Lack of consultation is a constitutional vice that vitiates tribunal's jurisdiction and public interest consistency.
propositions.quote: Lack of consultation amounts to a constitutional vice that vitiates the tribunal’s jurisdiction and, in the case before us, makes it inconsistent with the public interest.

propositions.text: Tribunal must rectify lack of consultation by engaging in missing consultation itself.
propositions.quote: In order to perform its duty, it must rectify the vice by itself engaging in the missing consultation.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues tribunals with legal jurisdiction must consider and fulfill consultation, as lack of consultation vitiates jurisdiction.

propositions.text: Court rejects argument that tribunal's power to consider law implies power to engage in consultation.
propositions.quote: This argument cannot be accepted, in my view.

propositions.text: Tribunal has only powers expressly or implicitly conferred by statute.
propositions.quote: A tribunal has only those powers that are expressly or implicitly conferred on it by statute.

propositions.text: Power to engage in consultation requires express or implied authorization beyond power to consider legal questions.
propositions.quote: In order for a tribunal to have the power to enter into interim resource consultations with a First Nation, pending the final settlement of claims, the tribunal must be expressly or impliedly authorized to do so.

propositions.text: Consultation is a distinct constitutional process involving facts, law, policy, and compromise, not merely a legal question.
propositions.quote: Consultation itself is not a question of law; it is a distinct and often complex constitutional process and, in certain circumstances, a right involving facts, law, policy, and compromise.

propositions.text: Tribunal must have remedial powers necessary to engage in consultation, depending on enabling statute and legislative intent.
propositions.quote: The tribunal seeking to engage in consultation itself must therefore possess remedial powers necessary to do what it is asked to do in connection with the consultation. The remedial powers of a tribunal will depend on that tribunal’s enabling statute, and will require discerning the legislative intent: Conway, at para. 82.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects that tribunals have inherent power to consult, requiring express authorization and remedial powers under enabling statute.

propositions.text: A tribunal with power to consider consultation adequacy but not to consult should provide appropriate relief under its statutory powers.
propositions.quote: A tribunal that has the power to consider the adequacy of consultation, but does not itself have the power to enter into consultations, should provide whatever relief it considers appropriate in the circumstances, in accordance with the remedial powers expressly or impliedly conferred upon it by statute.

propositions.text: The goal of such relief is to protect Aboriginal rights and promote reconciliation per Haida Nation.
propositions.quote: The goal is to protect Aboriginal rights and interests and to promote the reconciliation of interests called for in Haida Nation.

paragraphs.summary: The court states tribunals with consultation power but no consultation authority must provide appropriate relief to protect Aboriginal rights and promote reconciliation per Haida Nation.

propositions.text: Tribunals' limited statutory powers raise concern governments may avoid duty to consult by limiting tribunal mandates.
propositions.quote: The fact that administrative tribunals are confined to the powers conferred on them by the legislature, and must confine their analysis and orders to the ambit of the questions before them on a particular application, admittedly raises the concern that governments may effectively avoid their duty to consult by limiting a tribunal’s statutory mandate.

propositions.text: If tribunals lack power to consider consultation or if power is split, governments might avoid the duty to consult.
propositions.quote: The fear is that if a tribunal is denied the power to consider consultation issues, or if the power to rule on consultation is split between tribunals so as to prevent any one from effectively dealing with consultation arising from particular government actions, the government might effectively be able to avoid its duty to consult.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes tribunals' limited powers may let governments avoid consultation duties by restricting tribunal mandates or splitting consultation powers.

propositions.text: B.C. Court of Appeal found duty to consult is constitutional, invoking honour of the Crown, and must be met.
propositions.quote: As the B.C. Court of Appeal rightly found, the duty to consult with Aboriginal groups, triggered when government decisions have the potential to adversely affect Aboriginal interests, is a constitutional duty invoking the honour of the Crown. It must be met.

propositions.text: If tribunal structure cannot address adverse impacts on Aboriginal interests, affected peoples must seek remedies in courts.
propositions.quote: If the tribunal structure set up by the legislature is incapable of dealing with a decision’s potential adverse impacts on Aboriginal interests, then the Aboriginal peoples affected must seek appropriate remedies in the courts: Haida Nation, at para. 51.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees with B.C. Court of Appeal that duty to consult is constitutional and unmet tribunal structures require court remedies.

propositions.text: Haida Nation states duty to consult is a legal question based on facts; some deference to tribunal fact findings is appropriate.
propositions.quote: The starting point is Haida Nation, at para. 61: The existence or extent of the duty to consult or accommodate is a legal question in the sense that it defines a legal duty. However, it is typically premised on an assessment of the facts. It follows that a degree of deference to the findings of fact of the initial adjudicator may be appropriate.

propositions.text: Absent legal error, tribunal may be better positioned than court; standard of review likely reasonableness for mixed fact and law.
propositions.quote: Absent error on legal issues, the tribunal may be in a better position to evaluate the issue than the reviewing court, and some degree of deference may be required. . . . Absent error on legal issues, the tribunal may be in a better position to evaluate the issue than the reviewing court, and some degree of deference may be required. In such a case, the standard of review is likely to be reasonableness.

propositions.text: Pure legal issues get correctness standard; mixed fact and law issues get reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: To the extent that the issue is one of pure law, and can be isolated from the issues of fact, the standard is correctness. However, where the two are inextricably entwined, the standard will likely be reasonableness . . . .

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Haida Nation's standard of review: reasonableness for mixed fact and law, correctness for pure law, with deference to tribunal fact findings.

propositions.text: Some deference is appropriate on mixed fact and law matters, invoking reasonableness standard.
propositions.quote: It is therefore clear that some deference is appropriate on matters of mixed fact and law, invoking the standard of reasonableness.

propositions.text: Legislative intention must be considered in determining standard of review: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa.
propositions.quote: This, of course, does not displace the need to take express legislative intention into account in determining the appropriate standard of review on particular issues: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Khosa, 2009 SCC 12, [2009] 1 S.C.R. 339.

propositions.text: It is necessary to consider Administrative Tribunals Act and Utilities Commission Act provisions to determine appropriate standard of review here.
propositions.quote: It follows that it is necessary in this case to consider the provisions of the Administrative Tribunals Act and the Utilities Commission Act in determining the appropriate standard of review, as will be discussed more fully below.

paragraphs.summary: The court states deference applies on mixed fact and law, legislative intent matters, and relevant statutes must be considered for standard of review.

propositions.text: Having reviewed law on duty to consult and tribunals' role, court returns to appeal questions.
propositions.quote: Having considered the law governing when a duty to consult arises and the role of tribunals in relation to the duty to consult, I return to the questions at issue on appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court returns to the appeal questions after reviewing law on duty to consult and tribunals' role.

propositions.text: First question: was consideration of duty to consult within Commission's mandate?
propositions.quote: The first question is whether consideration of the duty to consult was within the mandate of the Commission.

propositions.text: Jurisdiction questions attract correctness standard of review; relevant statutes do not displace this.
propositions.quote: This being an issue of jurisdiction, the standard of review at common law is correctness. The relevant statutes, discussed earlier, do not displace that standard.

propositions.text: Court agrees with Court of Appeal that Commission did not err in concluding it had power to consider consultation issue.
propositions.quote: I therefore agree with the Court of Appeal that the Commission did not err in concluding that it had the power to consider the issue of consultation.

paragraphs.summary: The court holds jurisdiction questions get correctness review and agrees Commission had power to consider consultation.

propositions.text: Consultation issues arise from s. 35 Constitution Act, 1982, giving them constitutional dimension.
propositions.quote: As discussed above, issues of consultation between the Crown and Aboriginal groups arise from s. 35 of the Constitution Act, 1982 . They therefore have a constitutional dimension.

propositions.text: Question is whether Commission had power to consider consultation issue given constitutional nature.
propositions.quote: The question is whether the Commission possessed the power to consider such an issue.

propositions.text: Tribunals are confined to powers conferred by legislature; must ask if Utilities Commission Act conferred power to consider consultation.
propositions.quote: As discussed, above, tribunals are confined to the powers conferred on them by the legislature: Conway. We must therefore ask whether the Utilities Commission Act conferred on the Commission the power to consider the issue of consultation, grounded as it is in the Constitution.

paragraphs.summary: The court frames the issue whether the Commission had power to consider consultation under the Utilities Commission Act given constitutional nature.

propositions.text: It is common ground that Utilities Commission Act empowers Commission to decide questions of law in public interest determinations.
propositions.quote: It is common ground that the Utilities Commission Act empowers the Commission to decide questions of law in the course of determining whether the 2007 EPA is in the public interest.

propositions.text: Power to decide questions of law implies power to decide constitutional issues unless legislature clearly excludes it.
propositions.quote: The power to decide questions of law implies a power to decide constitutional issues that are properly before it, absent a clear demonstration that the legislature intended to exclude such jurisdiction from the tribunal’s power (Conway, at para. 81; Paul v. British Columbia (Forest Appeals Commission), 2003 SCC 55, [2003] 2 S.C.R. 585, at para. 39).

propositions.text: Specialized tribunals with expertise and authority are best positioned to decide constitutional questions related to their mandates.
propositions.quote: “[S]pecialized tribunals with both the expertise and authority to decide questions of law are in the best position to hear and decide constitutional questions related to their statutory mandates”: Conway, at para. 6.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Utilities Commission Act empowers the Commission to decide law questions, including constitutional ones unless excluded, and specialized tribunals are best positioned.

propositions.text: Section 71 factors focus mainly on economic issues but are broad enough to include Crown consultation with Aboriginal groups.
propositions.quote: Beyond its general power to consider questions of law, the factors the Commission is required to consider under s. 71 of the Utilities Commission Act, while focused mainly on economic issues, are broad enough to include the issue of Crown consultation with Aboriginal groups.
